full_answer:
# Risk assessment: reforestation finance in southern Spain

**Bottom line:** Of the 13 provinces compared, **Ciudad Real, Sevilla, Córdoba and Albacete** carry the lowest combined risk. They have a high share of land that qualifies for CO2 projects and the lowest average gully-erosion probability. Huelva, Almería, Alicante and Granada have the weakest profile.

## 1. Data and method
- **CO2 eligibility:** `co2_spain_legislation` (2026). This maps land that is suitable for CO2 absorption projects under MITECO rules for the carbon footprint registry. It has three classes: Eligible, Eligible with conditions, and Not eligible.
- **Erosion risk:** `rf_gully_probability` (2022). This is a model-estimated probability (%) that gullies are present. I used each province's average value.
- **Provinces included:** the 8 Andalusian provinces, plus Murcia and Alicante, plus Badajoz, Ciudad Real and Albacete, which lie in the south-centre and south-west. "Southern Spain" isn't formally defined, so I drew it broadly.
- **Combined ranking:** I added each province's rank for % Eligible (higher is better) to its rank for average gully probability (lower is better). This is a simple screening method I chose, not an official index.

## 2. Results

| # | Province | Eligible % | Eligible with conditions % | Not eligible %* | Avg gully prob. % | Rank sum | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ciudad Real | 78.9 | 12.8 | 8.3 | 47.8 | 2 | 🟢 Low |
| 2 | Sevilla | 73.2 | 15.5 | 11.3 | 50.5 | 6 | 🟢 Low |
| 3 | Albacete | 72.9 | 13.4 | 13.7 | 51.7 | 8 | 🟢 Low |
| 4 | Córdoba | 68.4 | 20.6 | 11.0 | 49.6 | 9 | 🟢 Low |
| 5 | Badajoz | 69.1 | 23.8 | 7.1 | 57.9 | 10 | 🟡 Moderate |
| 6 | Jaén | 58.4 | 22.8 | 18.8 | 49.2 | 13 | 🟡 Moderate |
| 6 | Murcia | 68.5 | 16.8 | 14.7 | 59.6 | 13 | 🟡 Moderate |
| 8 | Málaga | 67.8 | 14.3 | 17.9 | 66.4 | 17 | 🟠 Elevated |
| 9 | Cádiz | 56.8 | 22.7 | 20.5 | 59.3 | 19 | 🟠 Elevated |
| 9 | Granada | 67.3 | 13.5 | 19.2 | 67.5 | 19 | 🟠 Elevated |
| 11 | Almería | 62.4 | 26.3 | 11.3 | 68.0 | 22 | 🔴 High |
| 11 | Alicante | 63.9 | 20.3 | 15.8 | 70.0 | 22 | 🔴 High |
| 11 | Huelva | 42.7 | 22.6 | 34.7 | 60.9 | 22 | 🔴 High |

*Calculated as 100 − Eligible − Eligible with conditions. I checked Sevilla (11.3%) and Córdoba (11.0%) directly against the raster.

Chart: `southern_spain_co2_eligibility_vs_mean_gully_erosion_probability.png`

## 3. Risk profiles

**🟢 Preferred tier**
- **Ciudad Real:** the best on both measures, with the highest eligible share (78.9%) and the lowest average gully probability (47.8%). It is in Castilla-La Mancha, so it only counts if the bank's mandate allows south-central Spain.
- **Sevilla:** the best Andalusian option. 73.2% of its land is eligible and only 11.3% is not eligible. It has the 4th-lowest erosion of the 13.
- **Córdoba:** has the 3rd-lowest erosion (49.6%). A further 20.6% of its land is eligible with conditions, which is extra potential but means more permitting work.
- **Albacete:** similar to Sevilla, but also outside Andalusia.

**🟡 Moderate tier**
- **Badajoz:** has the smallest not-eligible share (7.1%), but higher erosion (57.9%).
- **Jaén:** has low erosion (49.2%), but only 58.4% of its land is fully eligible.
- **Murcia:** has good eligibility (68.5%) and medium erosion (59.6%).

**🔴 Avoid or impose strict conditions**
- **Huelva:** has the lowest eligibility (42.7%) and the highest not-eligible share (34.7%).
- **Almería and Alicante:** have the highest erosion (68–70%). This raises the risk that seedlings die and soil is lost, which would put credit delivery at risk.

## 4. Caveats for the bank
1. **Erosion is very uneven within provinces.** In Sevilla the average gully probability is 50.5% but the median is 24.3%, with a standard deviation of 43.1. Córdoba is similar: average 49.6%, median 25.9%. Most land has low gully probability, with concentrated hotspots, so each project site needs to be screened individually.
2. **The maximum erosion value doesn't help rank provinces.** Every province has a maximum of 100.4%, so the comparison uses only the average.
3. **"Return potential" here only means how much land is eligible.** The data don't include sequestration rates, land prices, water availability, fire risk or carbon prices. These need separate due diligence.
4. **"Eligible with conditions" land** (12.8–26.3% depending on the province) can add usable area, but it comes with regulatory conditions that the data don't describe.

**Suggested approach:** start the portfolio in Sevilla and Córdoba, or in Ciudad Real if the mandate allows it. Screen every site at municipal or plot level using the gully-probability layer.

description: Deep dive into Faro: BigEarthNet land cover + erosion interpretation
answer_preview: I can describe Faro's land cover, but the data can't show how gully risk relates to vegetation. The two layers can't be linked location by location, and the gully statistics for Faro look unreliable.
full_answer:
I can describe Faro's land cover, but the data can't show how gully risk relates to vegetation. The two layers can't be linked location by location, and the gully statistics for Faro look unreliable.

## 1. Land cover in Faro (BigEarthNet V2, 2018 – 6,767 labelled patches)

| Class | Faro | Beja (neighbouring district, for comparison) |
|---|---|---|
| Shrubland | **39.6 %** | 36.0 % |
| Broadleaf Forest | **35.0 %** | 33.8 % |
| Water | 9.8 % | 14.0 % |
| Grassland | 8.2 % | 8.8 % |
| Urban | 4.7 % | 3.9 % |
| Coniferous Forest | 2.0 % | 2.7 % |
| Sparse Vegetation | 0.7 % | 0.8 % |

- Shrubland and broadleaf forest together make up about 75 % of the patches. The landscape is mostly semi-natural woody cover: shrubs mixed with broadleaf trees.
- Conifers (2.0 %) and sparse vegetation (0.7 %) are rare. Very little of the district is bare or nearly bare.
- Faro has more urban cover (4.7 %) than Beja (3.9 %), and less water (9.8 % vs 14.0 %).

## 2. Gully erosion probability (Random Forest model trained on LUCAS 2022 field data)

| Statistic | Faro | Beja |
|---|---|---|
| Mean | 62.5 % | 42.0 % |
| Median | **100.4 %** | 15.3 % |
| Std. deviation | 43.3 | 42.9 |
| Min / max | 0 / 100.4 % | 0 / 100.4 % |
| Pixels | 1,416,386 | 2,715,090 |

**Caution:** a probability can't be 100.4 %. In Faro the median equals the maximum, so more than half of the pixels have exactly this value. That looks much more like a fill value, a no-data code or a saturated value than a real erosion probability. A clipping problem at the coast is also possible, since Faro's boundary box extends into the sea. The tools didn't confirm any of these explanations. So I wouldn't read Faro's mean of 62.5 % as a real risk level. Beja's median of 15.3 % suggests typical values in the region are much lower, but that's an inference, not a measurement.

## 3. How gully risk relates to vegetation: not answerable with this data

- The BigEarthNet layer is only available as percentages for the whole district. It doesn't say where each class is.
- So the gully probability can't be cross-tabulated by land-cover class, for example "gully risk under shrubland vs. forest".
- With only two districts, which have very similar land cover, comparing them doesn't show a statistical link either.
- The datasets also come from different years (2018 vs. 2022).

## 4. Land management perspective (with these limits)

Supported by the data:
- About 40 % of Faro is shrubland and 35 % broadleaf forest. That makes keeping this cover in place, and managing it, the main lever for protecting the soil.
- Grassland (8.2 %) and sparse vegetation (0.7 %) are the classes with the least permanent cover. In general erosion science these are the most exposed areas. That is general knowledge, not a result of this analysis.

Not supported:
- Whether gully risk is higher under shrubland or forest.
- How large an area is actually at high gully risk.

## Next steps
1. Check whether 100.4 is a no-data or fill value in the gully raster, and repeat the statistics without it.
2. Get a land-cover layer that shows where each class is (for example COS or CORINE). Only then can gully probability be summarised by class.
3. For field planning, focus checks on grassland and sparse-vegetation areas, and on shrubland after fires.

description: Comprehensive side-by-side deep dive of two provinces for a 10-year carbon project decision
answer_preview:
Cáceres is the better choice for a 10-year carbon sequestration project. It has more eligible land and a lower risk of gully erosion than Huelva.

## What the comparison covers
"All indicators" means
full_answer:
Cáceres is the better choice for a 10-year carbon sequestration project. It has more eligible land and a lower risk of gully erosion than Huelva.

## What the comparison covers
"All indicators" means two layers here, because only two of the available datasets cover Spain:
- **CO₂ project suitability (2026):** based on the Spanish environment ministry's (MITECO) criteria for registering carbon absorption projects.
- **Gully erosion probability (2022):** a modelled estimate of how likely gullies are, built from the EU's 2022 LUCAS field survey.

The third layer, a land-cover dataset (BigEarthNet), only covers Portugal, so I left it out. I have no data on soils, climate, water, wildfires, land use or protected areas for these two provinces, so this is not a full environmental assessment.

## Side-by-side results

| Indicator | Huelva | Cáceres |
|---|---|---|
| **CO₂: Eligible** | 42.7 % (#45 of 52 provinces) | **58.8 %** (#25 of 52) |
| **CO₂: Eligible with conditions** | 22.6 % | 29.8 % |
| **CO₂: Not eligible** | 34.7 % | **11.4 %** |
| **Eligible + conditional** | 65.3 % | **88.6 %** |
| **Gully probability: mean** | 60.9 % (#23 of 50, higher risk) | **50.1 %** (#43 of 50, lower risk) |
| **Gully probability: median** | 100.4 % | **18.8 %** |
| Gully probability: std. dev. | 43.7 | 44.5 |

The gully rank is out of 50 because that ranking table lists only 50 provinces.

**Huelva**
- Just over a third of the province is excluded from CO₂ projects, among the highest shares in Spain.
- Its median gully probability is at the maximum value. That means more than half the area falls in the highest gully class.

**Cáceres**
- Almost 9 in 10 pixels are eligible or conditionally eligible. In area terms, that's about 1.17 million fully eligible pixels against 0.43 million in Huelva, roughly 2.7 times as many.
- Erosion risk is moderate: it ranks among the 10 lowest provinces for mean gully probability. The low median and high standard deviation suggest the risk is concentrated in specific zones rather than spread across the province.

## Caveats on the erosion data
- The maximum and median values of 100.4 % are physically impossible. They are probably a scaling artifact (the 0–255 pixel values converted to percent).
- The erosion layer counts about twice as many pixels as the CO₂ layer for the same province. The highest erosion scores also belong to Baleares, Melilla and Ceuta (86–90 %). Both points suggest the province totals may include sea or no-data pixels. That could push up coastal Huelva's figures in particular.
- So treat the Huelva vs. Cáceres erosion comparison as a direction, not exact values.

## Recommendation for a 10-year sequestration project
1. **Eligibility and land base:** Cáceres has far more land that meets the registration criteria and much less excluded land. That makes it easier to find large, continuous plots.
2. **How long the carbon stays put:** lower gully risk means less chance of losing soil, seedlings and stored carbon over 10 years.
3. **In practice:** focus on the fully eligible areas in Cáceres and avoid the high-erosion pockets. If you use conditionally eligible land (29.8 %), check the specific MITECO conditions that apply.

**Before you commit:** confirm the decision with data I don't have, especially wildfire risk, water availability, land ownership and protected-area rules. Choosing exact sites would also need analysis at the municipality level.

I also made a chart comparing the two provinces: `huelva_vs_c_ceres_co2_eligibility_and_gully_probability.png`

description: Compare Setubal and Faro forest cover using BigEarthNet LULC with chart
answer_preview:
Setúbal has more forest than Faro, both as a share of its land and in total.

**Forest cover in BigEarthNet V2 (2018)**

| Class | Setúbal | Faro |
|---|---|---|
| Coniferous Forest | 8.1 % | 2.0 % |
full_answer:
Setúbal has more forest than Faro, both as a share of its land and in total.

**Forest cover in BigEarthNet V2 (2018)**

| Class | Setúbal | Faro |
|---|---|---|
| Coniferous Forest | 8.1 % | 2.0 % |
| Broadleaf Forest | 50.0 % | 35.0 % |
| **Total forest** | **58.1 %** | **37.0 %** |
| Labelled patches | 12,928 | 6,767 |
| Forest patches (approx.)* | ~7,510 | ~2,500 |

\*I estimated these by multiplying each district's patch total by its forest percentage. The tool returned rounded percentages, so the counts are approximate.

- **Share of land:** Forest makes up 58.1 % of Setúbal's patches and 37.0 % of Faro's. Setúbal is higher by about 21 percentage points.
- **Total forest:** Setúbal has about 7,510 forest patches and Faro about 2,500, so Setúbal has roughly three times as much. Setúbal also has nearly twice as many labelled patches overall.
- **Forest type:** Broadleaf forest is the main type in both districts. Coniferous forest is a small share, especially in Faro (2.0 %).
- **Faro's main cover:** Shrubland is Faro's largest class at 39.6 %, ahead of its total forest (37.0 %). In Setúbal, shrubland is 15.8 %.

**Limitations:**
- The data counts labelled Sentinel-2 image patches, not hectares, so this compares patch counts rather than exact area.
- A patch in BigEarthNet can carry more than one label. The percentages may therefore be shares of labels rather than of land, and adding coniferous and broadleaf forest may count some patches twice.
- How many patches a district has depends on how much of it the dataset covers, not only on the district's size.

full_answer:
I can't say which district has more Coniferous Forest or by how much. None of the tools would give me land-cover figures for either Lisboa or Leiria.

**The data exists.** The `bigearthnet_lulc` layer (BigEarthNet V2, 2018) covers both districts and has a "Coniferous Forest" class (value 1). The layer's description says it holds land-cover shares for each Portuguese district.

**Every attempt to read it failed:**
- **Comparing the two districts** (`compare_areas`): "Lisboa" wasn't found, and "Leiria" was read as the Spanish province Lleida.
- **Multi-layer analysis by name** (`analyze_multi_layer`): the same two failures.
- **Area analysis** (`analyze_area`): I tried the district outline the system adds after a lookup, Lisboa's full bounding box (-9.5, 38.67 to -8.79, 39.32) and small boxes drawn inside each district. Every time the error was "Could not determine district name from AOI".

This looks like a problem in how the tools match an area to a Portuguese district, not missing data. Someone who maintains the tools would need to fix that matching, or add a way to name a district directly. Once that works, the comparison is a single call, and I can rerun it.

**What I found:**
- The only land-cover layer is `bigearthnet_lulc` (BigEarthNet V2, 2018). It has 7 classes, and value 2 is "Broadleaf Forest". It lists Portalegre and Leiria among the 9 Portuguese districts it covers, so the data should exist.

- **Leiria by name:** I couldn't load it on its own at all. The province lookup returned Lleida, and the municipality lookup returned Llíria (Valencia).

The tools can't currently link an area to a Portuguese district for this layer, so I can't get the class shares. If you can get the district values another way, for example from the BigEarthNet district summary directly, I'll check them with you.

full_answer:
Six of the eight districts I could check have Broadleaf Forest cover above 30%. Leiria is the ninth district, and I couldn't get its figure, so the full answer is **6 or 7**.

The data come from the BigEarthNet V2 land cover layer for 2018, given as the share of image patches in each district.

| District | Broadleaf Forest | > 30% |
|---|---|---|
| Portalegre | 62.0% | ✅ |
| Setúbal | 50.0% | ✅ |
| Évora | 43.9% | ✅ |
| Santarém | 38.2% | ✅ |
| Faro | 35.0% | ✅ |
| Beja | 33.8% | ✅ |
| Castelo Branco | 28.9% | ❌ |
| Lisboa | 22.1% | ❌ |
| Leiria | not available | ? |

**Districts above 30%:** Portalegre, Setúbal, Évora, Santarém, Faro and Beja.

**Why Leiria is missing:** the layer includes Leiria, but the tools wouldn't return its data. Searching for "Leiria" kept matching Lleida, a province in Spain. Other spellings and a hand-drawn area inside the district also failed. I don't have Leiria's figure, so I can't say which side of 30% it falls on.
